questions.q: List the six celebrity writers quoted in Part I of "The Interview" and state each one's attitude toward being interviewed (positive, negative, or ambivalent) in one phrase per person.
questions.a: V.S. Naipaul: negative (feels wounded, loses part of self); Lewis Carroll: negative (horror of interviewer, refuses); Rudyard Kipling: strongly negative (calls it immoral, crime, assault, cowardly); H.G. Wells: ambivalent (calls it "ordeal" but does it frequently); Saul Bellow: negative (thumbprints on windpipe); Denis Brian: positive (supremely serviceable, gives interviewer unprecedented power). A wrong answer (e.g., missing names, misattributing views) reveals the student has not distinguished the polyphonic structure of Part I — the text deliberately assembles a chorus of conflicting opinions to establish the interview as a contested genre before Eco enters.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Christopher Silvester includes six different celebrity opinions before introducing Umberto Eco's interview in Part II. What argument about the interview genre does this arrangement build?
questions.a: Silvester uses the six voices to establish that the interview is a polarizing, morally ambiguous genre — not a neutral tool. The spectrum from Kipling's "crime/assault" to Brian's "supremely serviceable medium" creates tension: the interview simultaneously violates privacy and delivers truth. This prepares the reader to evaluate Eco's interview not as a routine Q&A but as a negotiated encounter where power, vulnerability, and artistry intersect. A wrong answer (e.g., "to show famous people have opinions") misses the structural purpose: the chorus frames the interview as a cultural problem, making Eco's comfortable engagement with it (Part II) a striking resolution.

questions.q: Mukund Padmanabhan uses two discourse linkers in the interview: "Which brings me to my next question" and "But let me tell you another story." Identify where each appears in the text and explain how each functions as a signaller that manages the conversation's flow.
questions.a: "Which brings me to my next question" appears when Mukund shifts from Eco's academic output to The Name of the Rose's success — it signals a topic transition while maintaining continuity (the "which" references the prior discussion of novels vs. scholarly work). "But let me tell you another story" appears when Eco deflects the question about medieval history's role in the novel's success — it signals a narrative digression that reframes the question as unanswerable. A wrong answer that only quotes the phrases without explaining their cohesive function reveals the student treats linkers as decoration rather than structural devices that reveal interviewer control and interviewee agency.

questions.q: Compare Rudyard Kipling's condemnation of interviews ("immoral," "crime," "assault") with his own action of interviewing Mark Twain. What does this contradiction reveal about the interview genre's power dynamics, and how does it foreshadow Eco's position in Part II?
questions.a: Kipling's hypocrisy exposes the interview's asymmetrical power: the interviewer holds authority (asking, publishing, framing), while the interviewee is vulnerable (exposed, quoted, potentially misrepresented). Kipling condemns the position of the interviewed but willingly occupies the interviewer's seat — proving the genre's allure for the questioner. This foreshadows Eco, who as interviewee in Part II reclaims agency by controlling narrative pace ("I work in interstices"), reframing questions ("Aah, now that is more difficult"), and telling stories on his terms. A wrong answer that calls Kipling merely "hypocritical" without analyzing the power asymmetry misses the text's central insight: the interview is a site of struggle over narrative control.

questions.q: Evaluate Denis Brian's claim that "the interviewer holds a position of unprecedented power and influence" against Saul Bellow's metaphor of interviews as "thumbprints on his windpipe." Which perspective does the text ultimately endorse, and what evidence from Part II supports your judgment?
questions.a: The text endorses a synthesis: the interviewer has institutional power (Brian), but a skilled interviewee can subvert it (Bellow/Eco). Evidence: Mukund asks, Eco redirects ("Maybe I give the impression..."), Mukund follows up, Eco controls tempo ("I work in empty spaces"), Mukund presses on fame, Eco reframes identity ("professor who writes novels on Sundays"). The interview becomes a collaboration, not an extraction. A wrong answer picking only Brian (power) or only Bellow (violation) fails to see the text's dialectic structure — Part I sets up the conflict, Part II resolves it in Eco's performative mastery.

questions.q: Write a 150-word character sketch of Mukund Padmanabhan as an interviewer, using only evidence from the text: his questions, his linkers, his knowledge of Eco's work, and Eco's responses to him. Focus on what his interviewing style reveals about his professionalism and preparation.
questions.a: Mukund Padmanabhan emerges as a prepared, respectful, and structurally adept interviewer. He opens with David Lodge's quote, proving he has read criticism on Eco. His questions progress logically: from Eco's productivity ("how does one man do all this?") to writing process ("interstices"), to style ("playful quality"), to identity ("novelist vs. professor"), to reception ("puzzled by success"), to causality ("medieval history?"). He uses signallers ("Which brings me...", "Could the huge success...") to transition smoothly. He corrects Eco's "20" to "Over 40" non-fiction works, showing fact-checking. Eco's laughter, expansive answers, and storytelling ("like a Chinese wise man") indicate comfort — Mukund creates safety, not "thumbprints on windpipe." A poor sketch lists questions without analyzing their sequence or Mukund's linguistic control, missing that the interviewer is a co-architect of the text's meaning.
